directions: Mountain ninebark is a compact Rocky Mountain native found on dry, rocky slopes, canyon walls, and open woodland edges from Colorado and Wyoming south into New Mexico, so it wants sharp drainage and shrugs off drought once its roots are established. Plant container stock in spring, siting it in full sun on a rocky bank, gravel garden, or unirrigated foundation bed where lusher shrubs struggle. Small domed clusters of white to pale pink flowers appear in early summer and are followed by papery reddish seed capsules, while older stems develop the same shredding, multi-layered bark typical of the genus. It needs almost no supplemental water or fertilizer after the first year and only occasional thinning of old stems to stay dense and tidy.

This is the western botanical variety of buttonbush recognized in California floras, growing as a large multi-stemmed shrub or small tree along foothill streambanks, seasonal creeks, and pond margins throughout the Central Valley and Coast Ranges. Plant it where soil stays consistently moist to seasonally saturated, such as a rain garden low point or pond edge, since it tolerates standing water far better than most woody plants. The spherical, pincushion-like white flower balls open in mid to late summer and draw heavy pollinator traffic, especially swallowtails and native bees, before maturing into round seed heads that persist for winter bird forage. Give it room to grow into a large, arching specimen and prune only to remove dead wood, since it blooms on new growth and recovers quickly from hard cutbacks if needed.

common_name: Albury Purple Tutsan (Purple-Foliage St. John's Wort)
directions: Albury Purple is a foliage-forward selection of tutsan grown as much for its wine-purple flushed leaves as for its small summer flowers, and the color deepens with cooler nights and a bit of direct sun exposure. Site it in part shade to morning-sun locations in humus-rich, evenly moist soil, where it forms a tidy rounded mound of semi-evergreen foliage that holds through mild winters. Loose clusters of small yellow flowers open through summer and are followed by berries that ripen from red through purple to nearly black, adding a second season of interest. Cut back hard in early spring if winter damages the foliage, since it resprouts readily from the base and rebuilds its mounded shape within one growing season.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)

directions: Elstead is grown chiefly for its abundant conical berries, which ripen from pale salmon through bright orange-red in late summer and hold on the stems for weeks, making it a favorite of cut-flower growers and flower arrangers as well as garden shrub borders. Plant in part shade to full sun in average, well-drained soil, where it forms an upright, bushy mound of blue-green leaves topped in midsummer by small clusters of five-petaled yellow flowers that give way to the showy fruit. It tolerates a fair amount of shade better than many flowering shrubs, making it useful under high canopy or on the north side of a border, though berry production is heaviest with at least a few hours of direct sun. Prune lightly in early spring to shape and remove any winter dieback, since flowers and berries form on the current season's growth.
